title: SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites 'Menon and Vondrick, 2022', but the reference list contains only 'Menon and Vondrick, 2023' (Visual classification via description from large language models). The year is inconsistent and no 2022 publication by the same authors appears in the bibliography.

The paper states that SAGE achieves 'as much as 14.6% relative precision improvement on state recognition for objects and actions unseen during training'. No table or result in the paper supports exactly 14.6%. The closest relative improvements computed from the tables are 13.95% (ChangeIt Novel Obj State Pre@1 vs. VidOSC) or 25% (HowToChange Novel Obj & Act Precision vs. VidOSC*). The claimed 14.6% is therefore unsubstantiated.

Runtime with Unknown Actions and Objects is claimed to be 7278.4 s for LFC and 612.7 s for VidOSC. With #Models 409 and runtime per model 18.2 s, LFC should be 18.2 × 409 = 7443.8 s. VidOSC with 20 models and 33.8 s per model gives 676.0 s. The reported numbers are arithmetically incorrect.

Several figure placeholders are present: '![Figure 10](image_10.jpg) <!-- Caption: Introduction, index 10 -->', 'Figure 19', 'Figure 25', 'Figure 40'. The actual figures are missing and the captions do not correspond to the figure numbers referenced in the text (Figure 1, 2, 3, 4, A1). The manuscript appears incomplete and the figures are not properly embedded.

The title reads 'SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S'. It appears truncated (likely missing 'tate-Action Graph Embedding'), creating an incomplete and erroneous title.

In Table 1, the asterisk (*) denotes 'Unified version implemented by us.' In Table 2, the same asterisk (*) denotes 'Results from the best specialized models.' The same symbol is used to convey different meanings between the tables, which is confusing and potentially misleading.

LFC (Souček et al., 2022) is a specialist model trained with pseudo-labels, yet its reported ChangeIt performance (State Pre@1 0.30, Trans. Pre@1 0.63) is identical to the zero-shot CLIP baseline (0.30, 0.63). It is highly improbable that a trained specialist yields exactly the same scores as a zero-shot model, suggesting a possible copy-paste or measurement error.
